title: Dresden Codex (Codex Dresdensis)
shelf_note: A facsimile of the Dresden Codex, a Maya screenfold. It belongs in the open-source/community collections. 'published: 1200' is a conventional approximate date.
structure_note: The structure counts give pages_translated 0, but pages_translated_field is 74, and this page does carry a translation. That looks like a counting or provenance mismatch (E2), not missing English. With 74 records for 74 codex pages, the record count fits. 'Leaf 34 = codex p. 55' fits a facsimile in Förstemann's page order (1–24, then 46–74, then 25–45), so it is not a sequencing error. No printed numbers, so no backsteps.

pages.layout: two registers split by a red rule; upper: two-column glyph block, a three-compartment caption box, a framed profile head at left, and to its right five numeral columns, three rows of day signs and red/black distance numbers; lower: two glyph rows over eight columns of bar-and-dot numerals (red zero shells), three rows of day signs and red/black distance numbers at the foot

tr_errors.source: - **Head:** a large profile head, black outline on the plain ground.
tr_errors.english: <note>- **Head:** a large profile head, black outline on the plain ground.
tr_errors.problem: Three body bullets of the figure description (Head, Frame, Panel) are wrapped in <note>. The reader then sees the page's own description styled as editorial apparatus, while the Identification and Colour bullets of the same list stay in the body.

other.note: The 'transcription' is a model-written structured reading in the first person, and the translation copies it into the reader text: 'I treat these as glyph affixes, not numerals.', 'Either I have missed a dot or the scribe left one out', 'I cannot confirm a Kin sign on the forehead'. It also includes PASS/FAIL arithmetic checks and comparisons with Förstemann's tables. It is openly labelled ('A structured reading by Claude Opus'), but model reasoning sits in the reading pane.

Nearly every glyph is given as 'unread glyph', now wrapped as <unclear>. The page is a numeral and day-sign reading with commentary, not a transcription of the hieroglyphic text. This is declared, not hidden.

items.quote: - **Head:** a large profile head, black outline on the plain

missing.english: Each group has three days, read top to bottom. The red coefficient stands to the left of each sign.
missing.why: Names like Muluc, Cimi and Ahau, and the numbers 1–13 in front of them, are days of the 260-day ritual calendar (tzolk'in). Nothing in the English says so.
The Maya count is base 20, except that the third place is 18×20 = 360. Without a note a reader cannot see why the places are 1, 20, 360, 7200, or check any total.
The page never says that 177 and 148 days are six and five lunar months, i.e. eclipse half-years. That is the whole point of the table.

missing.english: Förstemann thinks this is probably God D (Itzamna)
missing.why: 'God D' is Schellhas's letter for a Maya deity in the codices. A general reader does not know the lettering system.

missing.english: *Series totals (black, with red shells for zero; four places: 7200s / 360s / 20s / 1s)*
missing.why: The shell glyph is the Maya sign for zero. A reader may take the 'red shells' as decoration.

book_verdict: This is a real Dresden Codex leaf: p. 55 of the eclipse table, matching the image in layout, picture, red/black distance numbers and zero shells. Its numerals and day-sign arithmetic hold together. The text is a first-person model commentary rather than a transcription, though, and the translation styles part of the body as a <note>, so an expert would flag the presentation.
